articles.title: Community laments 'terribly sad' Sterts Theatre closure
articles.summary: Supporters say the venue showcased the best of local Cornish talent over 40 years.
articles.body:
Performers and show goers across Cornwall have said they were "devastated" to learn about the closure of a community theatre.

On Wednesday, Sterts Theatre CIC said it would be placed into creditors' voluntary liquidation amid an "exceptionally challenging time for cultural and arts organisations".

Nicky Brice, former ballet teacher at the theatre at Upton Cross on the edge of Bodmin Moor, said it was a "huge loss" for the area.

Former trustee, Ali Fenn, said she was "very saddened" by the closure, adding it had been a "fantastic asset in south east Cornwall" for young people.

"I hope, my heart seriously hopes and I'm sure everyone would say the same, we really, really hope that there is some future for the theatre, for the site, for Sterts," she said.

Brice, who taught at the theatre for 25 years, said its closure was "heart-breaking".

"It's an iconic theatre that showcased the best of local Cornish talent," she said.

Rebecca Mordan from Scary Little Girls theatre company has performed on its stage previously and said it was an "amazing venue".

"I'm just devastated and I think it's terribly sad," she said.

The theatre was founded in 1986, and had been significantly renovated in recent years after major damage from storms and hot weather .

Playwright Laura Horton, who has had shows including Cinderella played at the theatre, said she was "really shocked" by the closure.

"You just felt the love for the sector there," she said.

"It's just really scary to think that something that brings so much joy to people's lives is being eroded."

Brice said the "sadness" in these situations was that people do not hear about these organisations "being in trouble until they're closing".

"I think it's maybe about finding ways to communicate how bad it is," she said.

"Because people will often come forward and say 'I would have gone to that venue a bit more'."

Paula Every, who was previously involved with the theatre in Upton Cross, said: "It's a lovely theatre now and it would be really sad if it wasn't used by the community which is who it should be being used by."

The BBC has contacted Sterts for further comment.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The National Investigation Agency (NIA) on Thursday arrested deported fugitive Harwinder Kumar @ Sonu, accused in the case related to the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The National Investigation Agency (NIA) on Thursday arrested deported fugitive Harwinder Kumar @ Sonu, accused in the case related to the targeted killing of VHP leader Vikas Prabhakar in 2024, from the UAE. Soon after landing at the Indira Gandhi International Airport here, he was placed under arrest by the NIA and later produced before the Special NIA court.Harwinder, who was based in the UAE and on the NIA's 'wanted' list, was allegedly involved in providing logistical support and financing to foreign-based perpetrators of the crime, affiliated with pro-Khalistan terrorist outfit Babbar Khalsa International (BKI).Prabhakar alias Vikas Bagga was shot dead in his confectionery shop at Nangal in Punjab's Roopnagar district on April 13, 2024. He was the Nangal president of the Vishva Hindu Parishad (VHP).The NIA took over the case from the state police on May 9. Investigation has found that Prabhakar was killed by members of the Babbar Khalsa International, as part of conspiracy hatched by Germany-based BKI operatives Harjit Singh alias Laddi and Kulbeer Singh alias Sidhu. Three chargesheets have been filed so far in the matter.NIA on Thursday said Harwinder was deported from the UAE to India after vigorous diplomatic efforts. His arrest follows that of another UAE-based accused, Manveer Ram, on Aug 13, 2026. Manveer, allegedly involved in supplying weapons used in the crime, was intercepted at Amritsar Airport and subsequently arrested by the NIA.NIA said Harwinder acted as both a recruiter and handler, arranged weapons and facilitated their delivery to the shooters involved in the killing Prabhakar. He also received and transferred terror funds in connection with the conspiracy, acting on the directions of Harjit Singh and Kulbeer Singh."The deportation of Harwinder from the UAE and his subsequent arrest by the NIA demonstrate the agency’s resolve to pursue fugitives involved in terrorism cases and bring them back to India to face the due process of law," NIA noted in its statement on Thursday.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Flydubai attacker 'underwent Islamist radical indoctrination', Netanyahu says
articles.summary: Israel's prime minister says the pilot who tried to take over the Flydubai plane clearly intended to "down the plane".
articles.body:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says investigations suggest the man who stabbed his fellow pilot and tried to take over a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".

The Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two hours into its journey on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control to land safely.

Netanyahu told Fox News that it was looking "very likely" that the attacker, who he said was an Omani national, "was going to down the plane".

Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) state news agency reports investigations have begun there to determine "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose".

The Interior Ministry of Saudi Arabia - where the plane made an emergency landing - said that both the pilot and co-pilot had been sent back to the UAE on Thursday morning after medical teams had cleared them.

UAE officials earlier claimed jurisdiction over the incident because the aircraft on which the attack took place is registered there and flies under its flag.

Netanyahu told Fox that once the attacker had been subdued and tied up by passengers and crew, he was "calling out to the aircrew 'kill me, kill me', so it's clear he was suicidal - that's not a question".

"And with all the passengers in there, and if you couple that with what I just told you about the Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that were found in his background, I think... that'll give us a pretty good clue."

However, he stressed that he did not want to draw any firm conclusions as to motive yet.

Pilots from countries without diplomatic relations with Israel were usually not allowed to fly there, Netanyahu said when asked about how the suspected Omani pilot came to be on the plane.

He added: "Obviously there was a loophole here and we're taking care of that among other things... with the full co-operation, I have to say, of the Emirati government, so we're both interested in making sure this doesn't happen again."

The prime minister was also asked earlier on the same network whether there was an indication if Iran was involved, he replied: "It's too early to say".

Flydubai passenger describes hugging his children as plane nosedived during attack

Who is the 'hero' Indian pilot who was stabbed on Israel-bound flight?

Both Netanyahu and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the stabbed pilot, Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar was a "hero".

India's ambassador to the UAE Deepak Mittal visited Captain Machhar in hospital on Thursday, the Indian Mission confirmed on social media, stating he was "in good health and recovering well".

Preliminary findings from a separate Israeli investigation into the incident, suggest that the alleged attacker intended to crash the plane, an Israeli security source told BBC Arabic.

The source said the investigation - led by Israel's intelligence agency Mossad - interviewed passengers after they arrived in Tel Aviv to establish what had happened on the plane.

Flydubai's flight FZ1073, with more than 170 people on board, took off from Dubai International Airport in the UAE at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time), en route to Ben Gurion Airport.

Two hours later, the 17,000ft drop in altitude was reported on the plane tracking website Flightradar24 and minutes later the plane signalled an emergency code.

At about 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent, landing safely at Tabuk Airport in the north west of Saudi.

Flydubai has since suspended flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv as it carried out its own investigation into the incident.

Israel's Transportation Ministry said the suspension aligns with Netanyahu's directive.

Israeli airlines including El Al, Israir and Arkia said plans were in place to operate rescue flights from Dubai starting on Friday to bring back stranded passengers.

The Transportation Ministry also said it sent an urgent request to Etihad Airlines to increase the number of flights between Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv.

articles.title: Grimmest climbing year since '15 as bad weather, risky calls kill 40
articles.summary: At least 40 climbers and expedition workers have died across Nepal’s Himalayas and PoK’s Karakoram since May this year, making 2026 the region’s deadliest
articles.body: At least 40 climbers and expedition workers have died across Nepal’s Himalayas and PoK’s Karakoram since May this year, making 2026 the region’s deadliest mountaineering year since 2015. Heavy snowfall and changing weather created hazardous conditions, but decisions to continue climbing or remain at exposed camps despite worsening weather also figured in several deaths. Two avalanches accounted for 26 fatalities; 10 were on Broad Peak (8,051m), including record-setting mountaineer Nirmal Purja and five other accomplished Nepalese climbers, and 16 at Himlung Himal (7,126m).High-altitude expedition safety analyst Dr Aris Thorne told TOI commercial considerations and record-setting attempts could complicate decisions to turn back. “When stakes are this high, climbers often gamble against the mountain's timeline rather than the weather forecast. We saw teams bypass obvious red flags because turning back means writing off thousands of dollars and months of logistical prep. It’s an unspoken hubris that treats safety margins as negotiable.”Veteran high-altitude alpine historian Vaughn Vance said: “The obsession with ticking off commercial milestones has blinded many to the reality of the death zone. When you have millions of dollars tied up in marketing campaigns and summit sponsorships, objective risk assessment gets thrown out the window.”Nepal has no strict qualification requirements for climbers attempting its peaks, an issue that has concerned experienced mountaineers. “You have to qualify to do the Ironman,” prominent Everest chronicler and climber Alan Arnette said. “But you don’t have to qualify to climb the highest mountains in the world?”On Manaslu (8,163m), Indian-origin climber Dhrubajyoti Guha and his guide, Fursemba Sherpa, continued towards Camp III while six others retreated amid worsening weather. Guha and Sherpa were later found buried inside their tent. “Six other climbers who decided to retreat from Camp 2 are safe,” Makalu Adventure managing director Mohan Lamsal had told TOI. He said the pair had headed higher for an early summit attempt. At Himlung Himal, 16 Nepalese expedition workers were killed in a Sept 27 avalanche while preparing base camp. Among them were a cook and kitchen assistant from the team of Imagine Nepal's Mingma Gyalje Sherpa, who led the rescue operation. “We could have saved lives today, but due to bad weather, we reached the accident site only in the evening,” he wrote on Instagram.Mingma said he had repeatedly urged the two workers to leave base camp as conditions deteriorated. “They came down briefly and then went back to base camp. They were swept away by the avalanche on Sunday morning,” he said.For high-altitude workers, however, leaving early can carry financial consequences. “People ask why the workers didn't just evacuate when the warnings came down,” Himalayan workers’ rights advocate Maya Sherpa said. “But for a high-altitude worker, leaving base camp early can mean losing seasonal wages, or worse, being branded as uncooperative by outfitters. They are often trapped between the wrath of a storm and the economic necessity of keeping the expedition alive.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Massachusetts couple represented themselves in a dispute over damaged trees and encroachments on their land; they won a $310,000 judgment against their neighbour, and an appeals court upheld it in 2026
articles.summary: A court dispute between neighbouring property owners in Massachusetts over damaged trees and illegal land encroachments has ended with a $310,000 judgment
articles.body: A court dispute between neighbouring property owners in Massachusetts over damaged trees and illegal land encroachments has ended with a $310,000 judgment upheld on appeal, after the affected couple successfully handled their own case without hiring lawyers. The ruling by the Massachusetts Appeals Court is a major success for people who represent themselves in court. It shows that self-represented property owners can handle complicated land disputes and win large monetary awards against neighbouring property owners. The case focused on property boundaries, unauthorised encroachments, and the cutting and damage of mature trees. Those actions triggered state laws that protect trees and can greatly increase damages for illegal tree cutting and trespass on private property.Boundary disputes and property damageThe dispute began when the Massachusetts homeowners found that their neighbour had changed property boundaries and made unauthorised structural and physical changes that reached onto their private land. Several trees on the homeowners' property were also cut down or damaged without their permission. Instead of taking no action or relying only on private efforts to settle the matter, the landowners brought the dispute to state court. They faced potentially high legal costs for hiring lawyers who handle land and property cases, so the couple decided to represent themselves during the trial. Under Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 242, Section 7, a person who cuts down or destroys trees on another person's land without legal permission can be required to pay the property owner three times the assessed damages. This applies when the act was intentional and done without good reason.Trial court findings and financial awardDuring the trial, the self-represented couple presented detailed survey records, evidence from the property, photographs, and property assessments. They used these materials to show where the property boundary was, what violations had occurred, and how much the damaged trees were worth. The trial judge reviewed the evidence and found that the neighbour had unlawfully encroached on the land. The judge also found that the destruction of the trees was willful, rather than accidental. Because state timber trespass law multiplies damages for tree destruction, and because the court also awarded money for property restoration and damage caused by the physical encroachments, the court entered a total judgment of $310,000 against the neighbour.Appeals court review and final judgmentThe neighbouring landowner was not satisfied with the trial result and filed an appeal with the Massachusetts Appeals Court. The appellant argued that the trial judge had made mistakes in finding the facts and that the $310,000 award was too high. In its written opinion, the Massachusetts Appeals Court rejected those arguments and upheld the trial court's judgment in full. The appellate panel found that the trial record contained enough evidence to support the judge's findings about the property boundaries, the intentional damage, and the value assigned to the destroyed trees. The appeals judges said that courts must generally respect the trial judge's decisions about witness credibility and findings of fact when those findings are supported by credible evidence in the record. Because the self-represented couple established the relevant facts and followed the applicable rules of evidence and civil procedure, the appeals court concluded that the $310,000 award should remain in place.Implications for self-represented litigantsLegal observers note that property and boundary cases in state courts can involve detailed surveys, expert evidence, property laws, and court procedures. This can make representing yourself especially difficult for people who are not lawyers. The appellate panel's decision confirms that self-represented litigants in Massachusetts must meet the same legal standards as licensed lawyers. It also shows that people representing themselves can succeed when their claims are supported by clear evidence and the laws that apply to their case. With the appeals court upholding the original judgment, the $310,000 award remains enforceable against the neighbour. That brings the multi-year dispute over the land to an end.You use AI every day. articles.title: Algeria introduces death penalty for arsonists after wildfires
articles.summary: It is estimated more than 200 people have died in blazes in the north-east of the country over the summer.
articles.body:
Algeria has adopted a law imposing the death penalty on people convicted of arson of forests or fields after a series of deadly wildfires swept parts of the country.

Members of the national assembly voted through the bill, which also made child abduction a capital offence, on Thursday.

Capital punishment has been in the country's penal code for some offences, but no execution has been carried out since 1993.

The official death toll from the blazes stands at 12, but independent news outlets believe the figure to be much higher.

Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune ordered the justice ministry to introduce the changes to the criminal law after more than 100 fires in the north-east of the country during an intense heatwave in northern Africa.

Under the law, anyone convicted of deliberately setting fire to forests, woods or fields could face execution.

The death penalty has also been extended to child kidnappings that involve torture, sexual assault or mutilation.

According to news agency AFP, Justice Minister Lotfi Boudjemaa told parliament: "The adoption of the death penalty for these acts is the appropriate legal response to curb these crimes."

The tougher penalties were justified because arson had reached "the level of organised crime", with investigations suggesting links to "foreign parties", Boudjemaa said.

The upper house, the Council of the Nation, will review the law before it is officially ratified by the president.

Investigative journalist Nozha Khelalef has been gathering the names of those believed to have died in the fires from death notices posted by families and information shared by some local authorities.

Her tally, listed on the independent news website Twala , puts the death toll at 200.

While Algeria regularly experiences forest fires in the summer, climate change has exacerbated the intensity and severity of recent wildfires in the country.

articles.title: In 2018, a Vermont couple started with 30 sheep; seven years later, their solar-grazing business had 500 sheep managing vegetation across 1,500 acres of solar sites in the Northeast
articles.summary: What started in 2018 as a small trial with just 30 sheep has grown into a commercial operation that now manages vegetation around thousands of solar
articles.body: What started in 2018 as a small trial with just 30 sheep has grown into a commercial operation that now manages vegetation around thousands of solar panels across the American Northeast. Husband-and-wife farmers Lewis Fox and Niko Kochendoerfer founded Agrivoltaic Solutions LLC in Vermont. They developed a model that uses livestock instead of mechanical mowers to control grass and weeds around solar energy sites. According to a case study published by the American Solar Grazing Association, the couple's business has grown from its first flock of 30 sheep to 500 sheep managing vegetation across 1,500 acres of solar sites. The operation shows how farming and renewable energy can work together. The model can provide steady income for regional livestock producers while lowering maintenance costs for energy companies.Scaling up operations across state bordersSolar grazing uses sheep to eat grass, weeds, and brush growing around ground-mounted solar arrays. Heavy machinery can damage electrical cables or solar panels. Mechanical mowing equipment can also throw rocks into glass solar components. Sheep, by comparison, can move easily under low-clearance solar racks. They can keep plant growth under control without putting sensitive electrical wiring at risk. When Fox and Kochendoerfer started Agrivoltaic Solutions in 2018, solar grazing was still an untested way to maintain solar sites in the region. After showing that sheep could reliably keep vegetation within height limits set by utility operators, the business grew quickly. As detailed on the company's official site, Agrivoltaic Solutions now manages contracted grazing operations in Vermont, New Hampshire, Maine, New York, Pennsylvania, and Illinois. Along with managing flocks directly, the company has created custom grazing plans for more than 30,000 acres of solar projects across the United States.Financial stability through dual land useFor traditional livestock farmers, finding affordable pasture and keeping income steady can be ongoing challenges. Land rental costs, changing meat prices, and seasonal weather changes can all reduce the profits of family farms. Combining sheep farming with solar sites offers another option by turning maintenance budgets into farm income. Instead of farmers paying to rent land for grazing, solar developers pay farmers to maintain their sites. This shared-use model gives farmers access to stable, multi-year contracts. It also lets them grow their herds without having to buy more land. According to research noted by the American Solar Grazing Association, solar grazing keeps maintenance spending within local farming communities. Instead of sending that money to commercial landscaping or mowing companies, utility operators pay regional livestock producers directly for the work. This approach can help small farms build stronger businesses. It also means land used for renewable energy can continue to support local agriculture.Collaborative networks and consulting expansionAs demand for solar maintenance grew beyond what their own 500 sheep could handle, Fox and Kochendoerfer expanded their business by bringing in other regional livestock producers. Through Agrivoltaic Solutions, the couple serves as a link between utility developers and independent local livestock owners. Under this system, nearby farms provide sheep and handle daily flock care. Agrivoltaic Solutions manages logistics, insurance requirements, site checks, and contracts with companies. This partner model allows smaller farms to take part in commercial solar contracts without taking on the administrative work or legal risks that can come with large utility sites. To help improve industry standards, the company also added professional consulting services to its grazing work. The firm works with solar developers, engineering companies, and land planners during the early stages of site development. The goal is to make sure new solar sites are designed with animal safety and handling in mind. Design details include setting panel wires at suitable heights, choosing seed mixes that work well for sheep during site restoration, installing suitable perimeter fencing, and providing reliable water for grazing animals. By including farming needs in renewable energy planning from the beginning, solar sites can be ready for livestock grazing as soon as construction is finished. This can create long-term partnerships between energy companies and rural farming communities.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Dual UK-Iranian national arrested over RAF Fairford incident
articles.summary: The 27-year-old man was arrested in Westminster, London, marking the sixth arrest in connection with Sunday's incident near the airbase.
articles.body:
A UK-Iranian dual national has been arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with the incident at RAF Fairford, counter-terror police have said.

The 27-year-old man was arrested in Westminster, London. A second man, a 26-year-old UK national, has also been questioned under caution, and two properties in the area have been searched.

Five men in their twenties who were arrested near the Gloucestershire airbase on Sunday remain on police bail. All five were UK nationals from London.

Counter-terror police are considering "all possible angles - including foreign state involvement", the force's senior national coordinator Vicki Evans said.

"The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry," she said.

"I'd like to thank the public for their continued support and patience whilst we work through this investigation."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday there were "strong indications" that Iran played a part in the incident. He did not provide further details, and Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.

The five men were arrested in the early hours of Sunday morning after "three suspicious vehicles" were reported travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF), sparking a major security incident.

The BBC understands that one of the men had dialled 999 himself, about an hour before a local farmer alerted police to a "large group" of masked men near the vehicles.

They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail on Monday in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".

Police said a quantity of petrol but no explosive devices were found during searches of vans near the site.

The group were aged between 23 and 25. Four live in Westminster and one in Camden, and searches of their homes were carried out.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that "the hands of a foreign actor" had clearly been involved in the incident at the base, which has been used as a forward operating location by the USAF for decades.

In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the airbase for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

articles.title: Residents' fears over 'monster' data centre
articles.summary: More than 100 residents attended the first consultation event.
articles.body:
More than 100 people attended a consultation on plans to build a large data centre on green belt land in Cheshire.

Innova held the drop-in session at High Legh Village Hall near Lymm on Wednesday evening to discuss plans to build a 60-hectare data centre in Little Bollington.

Local resident Mike Reed, who is helping to organise local opposition to the plan, described it as a "massive great industrial monster" and said locals left the meeting with "deep anxiety" over the potential impact on their homes, businesses and wildlife.

The company said it was "pleased with the turnout" and "grateful to local residents for providing valuable feedback".

Data centres are typically large warehouses that store servers which process and distribute information online.

The proposed Spodegreen Data Centre would occupy land owned by the Tatton Estate.

At the first public consultation, Reed said: "People are very upset at this proposal.

"It's green belt land at the edge of Manchester's conurbation.

"You can't start creeping into that, or you destroy the whole of the green belt throughout Cheshire."

Another resident, Helen Dolan, expressed her concern over noise levels and the threat to wildlife.

A spokesperson for Innova said: "We were pleased with the turnout at last night's first consultation event and grateful to local residents for providing valuable feedback around water, noise, landscape, drainage and green belt in particular.

"The technical assessments that will provide detailed answers to these questions, including those on noise, water use and energy demand, are being undertaken."

Innova added the project would bring benefits to the area, including jobs, improved local connectivity and money from the Community Benefit Fund, which the company said would "specifically direct funds locally where it is needed".

The next stage of the process will involve a second in-person consultation event later this year, according to the Innova website.

The company said it will share how the project has evolved after consultation feedback and environmental assessments.

articles.title: US filmmaker Hopwood DePree loses High Court battle against council over ancestral 60-room mansion; after securing Hopwood Hall for £1, he spent £750,000 restoring it before being locked out in 2024
articles.summary: American filmmaker Hopwood DePree has lost his High Court battle to regain access to his ancestral 60-room mansion in England, ending a long-running
articles.body: American filmmaker Hopwood DePree has lost his High Court battle to regain access to his ancestral 60-room mansion in England, ending a long-running dispute with Rochdale Borough Council over the future of the historic property.DePree, 56, had spent almost a decade trying to restore the 15th-century Hopwood Hall in Middleton after believing he had secured the property for just £1. According to SWNS, he invested around £750,000 in repairs and restoration work before the council barred him from the building in 2024.The legal dispute centred on planning permission and the terms of an agreement reached between DePree and the council in 2017.How the £1 deal for Hopwood Hall came aboutDePree began working on the restoration project in 2013, motivated in part by family stories about his ancestors living at the historic manor.By 2017, an agreement had been reached under which Hopwood Hall would be transferred to DePree for £1 once the necessary planning permission had been secured.Encouraged by the agreement, DePree settled in the UK, established the Hopwood Foundation and began working to revive the Grade II-listed building.The hall had stood derelict for decades, with broken windows and leaking walls. The cost of fully restoring the property has been estimated at between £30 million and £40 million.Planning permission became the centre of the disputeThe property subsequently became the subject of a dispute over how it should ultimately be used.DePree envisioned using the restored hall for events, weddings and tours, while the council wanted the historic property to serve the wider community.In October 2022, planning permission was granted for the site to accommodate events, hospitality, tours, education, cafés and shops.However, the court heard that the 2017 transfer agreement was no longer considered sufficient following changes to the planning permission. A second transfer application was therefore required.That application was never made, and in 2024 Rochdale Borough Council closed the property to DePree.Council and filmmaker offered different interpretations of the agreementThe dispute eventually escalated into a High Court case, with both sides presenting different interpretations of the original agreement.The council argued that DePree's planning application did not go far enough to constitute the detailed planning permission required for the proposed refurbishment. It also argued that he had failed to provide an adequate business plan, a claim DePree disputed.DePree's legal team, meanwhile, argued that the 2017 agreement did not require planning permission covering every element of the extensive restoration project. They maintained that the work was always intended to progress in stages and that the council had failed to honour its obligation to transfer the hall.The High Court ultimately ruled against DePree.Judge acknowledges DePree’s commitment to the restorationDuring the judgment, Judge Hodge acknowledged DePree's commitment to the historic property.The judge said that during his cross-examination, “there was no disguise to his enthusiasm or commitment to bringing Hopwood back to life”.However, the judge also found that DePree did not answer questions properly when he was being pressed during the proceedings.The filmmaker is expected to appeal the decision, the court heard.The case has also left DePree facing substantial legal costs, reportedly estimated at between £70,000 and £114,000.Council says Hopwood Hall should benefit the wider communityFollowing the judgment, a spokesperson for Rochdale Borough Council said it was pleased with the outcome but described the legal battle as costly.“We are pleased with the judgement but it is a shame that we had to endure a costly court battle,” the spokesperson said.The council added that Hopwood Hall would be “used for the benefit of the wider community”.DePree, meanwhile, described the ruling as a major disappointment for those who had supported the restoration effort.“This is of course incredibly disappointing and a huge blow to our community, our supporters around the world, as well as the UK’s charitable heritage rescue groups in general,” he said.For nearly a decade, DePree's campaign to save Hopwood Hall had brought international attention to the neglected historic property. The High Court ruling now leaves the future ownership and restoration of the 15th-century mansion in the hands of the council, subject to any appeal.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Man who took Fairford arrest picture says 'all hell broke loose'
articles.summary: The man who took the famous arrest image says the military is not doing enough to reassure locals.
articles.body:
The man who took a now-famous photo of the five men arrested at RAF Fairford said he thought nothing of it until he woke up the following morning.

"I saw the guys being arrested outside the house on Sunday morning and went back to bed and thought, 'oh, well they've got them now'," said the Whelford resident, who did not want to be named. "Then all hell broke loose at half past six in the morning."

At a police information point at Fairford Community Centre earlier, he - along with other locals - said communication from the military base following the major security incident had been "poor".

The US Air Force, which operates from RAF Fairford, has been approached for comment.

A major investigation was launched after five men were arrested at RAF Fairford on Sunday on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act. They have since been bailed.

Earlier, Counter Terrorism Policing announced a 25-year-old man, a dual UK-Iranian national, had been arrested in London , on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts.

It follows the prime minister commenting on Wednesday that he believed Iran was involved in the Fairford incident.

The man who took the widely shared image said police did not have enough information at Thursday's drop-in event "to be able to give us anything".

"Going forward, whats going to happen?" said the resident of Whelford, which is next to the RAF base.

"Recently I think [the base's] communication with the local population has been poor.

"I can see why people do feel unsafe," he added.

Another local, Selina Vesey-Hague, said representatives from the military base should have been at the police event to answer questions.

"I think obviously a lot of people think it could happen again. And so we need a proper, proper plan," she said.

When asked if she felt reassured, Vesey-Hague said "possibly not".

"I wouldn't say I feel particularly safe," she added.

Event stopped after 'abuse' over beauty spot plans

'Shameful' delays lead to people collecting own mail

Families welcome right to challenge A&E care

A Whelford resident told the BBC she was not surprised there were suspicions over Iranian involvement, and there was "a lot of resentment" in the village.

"None of us wanted the American bombers here. We don't mind the base, but not this bombing campaign."

She added: "As a village we're feeling a bit lost and ignored by the machinations of what's going on with the police and the base.

"There are 85 homes here with people of varying ages and frailties.

"We'd like a lot of answers about why the MOD phone wasn't answered [as the incident unfolded]. If security was increased on Saturday as it was then why were notices not issued to residents?"

PC Tyler Harris from Gloucestershire Police said the public sessions were set up because "it's a major thing that's happened and everyone's got lots of questions, and emotions can be up in the air".

He said the community had been "very understanding" that the force can "only talk about certain things".

Harris said officers would be doing "high-visibility patrols" in the area and that letters had been sent out to the households closest to the incident.

There will be more police drop-in events set up over the next couple of weeks, he added.

Michael Vann, district councillor for Fairford, called the meeting "very much a first step", if a "tiny bit belated".

He added: "There was an elephant in the room who wasn't there - the United States Air Force."

Vann said a regular meeting held on Wednesday evenings at the base had been cancelled.

"Theres a big difference between being safe and feeling safe," said Cotswold District councillor Tristan Wilkinson.

"I have every reassurance from the authorities about the measures they're taking to keep the community safe - that's very different from people feeling safe.

"People don't feel safe," he said, adding one person told the meeting: "We feel like sitting ducks."

"They need to be told really clearly what the authorities are doing to protect this community," said Wilkinson.

"As long as this conflict with Iran goes on we will be living next door to a significant military base, and we need to be planning for the long term.

"We need to figure out how we live side-by-side so that they [the base] have the operational independence they need but also how the community is reassured."

articles.title: An American artist traded a painting and $10 for a 153-acre Connecticut farm in 1882; more than a century later, his home and studios became part of a nationally protected landscape devoted to art
articles.summary: Discover how Julian Alden Weir transformed a simple painting and $10 into a 153-acre Connecticut farm, becoming a pivotal part of American Impressionism at Weir Farm National Historical Park.
articles.body: A painting that once cost American artist Julian Alden Weir $560 ended up helping him acquire something far more lasting, a 153-acre farm in Connecticut.In July 1882, Weir exchanged the painting and $10 for the Branchville property, a deal that would shape much of the rest of his artistic life. He went on to make the farm his primary residence for the next 36 years, building a studio there and using its fields, woods and rocky landscape as subjects for his work.More than a century later, the property became part of Weir Farm National Historical Park, preserving the home, studio and landscape where Weir and other artists worked. The National Park Service describes the site as the only National Historical Park dedicated to preserving the home, studio and grounds of a late 19th-century American artist.The original 153-acre farm has since been reduced in size, with the present-day park encompassing a 68-acre site. But the connection between the landscape and the art created there remains central to the park.The unusual deal that changed Weir's lifeThe story began when art collector Erwin Davis wanted a painting Weir had acquired in Europe.At the time, Weir was living in New York, working as a portrait and still-life painter, teaching at the Art Students League and buying art for himself and other collectors.Davis offered him a farm in Branchville in exchange for the painting and an additional $10.Weir travelled to see the property before making his decision. In a June 1882 letter to his fiancée, Anna Dwight Baker, he wrote that he wanted to see whether the acreage was habitable and whether it could serve as a retreat.On July 19, 1882, the deal was completed. Weir received the Branchville farm in exchange for the painting and $10.What may initially have looked like a simple retreat soon became much more important to the artist.After marrying Baker the following year, Weir returned to the United States from their honeymoon in Europe and made Branchville his primary residence for the next three and a half decades.Who was Julian Alden Weir?Born on August 30, 1852, in West Point, New York, according to NPS, Weir grew up in a family deeply connected to art.His father, Robert Walter Weir, was a painter and professor of drawing at the US Military Academy. His older brother, John Ferguson Weir, also became a prominent artist and later served as the first director of the Yale School of Fine Arts.Julian enrolled at New York's National Academy of Design at 17 before travelling to Europe. Between 1873 and 1877, he studied primarily at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris, where he also studied under painter Jean-Léon Gérôme.After returning to New York, Weir established himself as a painter and teacher. His work initially focused on portraits and still lifes, but his approach changed after he settled at Branchville.The Connecticut landscape gradually became central to his work.The farm became his artistic laboratoryAt Branchville, Weir began moving away from the conventional artistic approach he had learned during his training.He experimented with etching and developed a more personal approach to landscape painting, drawing influence from Japanese art and French Impressionism.The farm provided him with an endless supply of subjects.Fields, trees, stone walls, barns and changing light appeared repeatedly in his work. The landscape was not simply the setting around his home. It became part of the way he thought about painting.Weir also built a studio on the property and expanded the farmhouse several times.The farm soon became a gathering place for other artists. Childe Hassam, John Twachtman, Albert Pinkham Ryder and other artists visited, spending time painting, fishing, hunting and discussing art.In the late 1890s, Weir and Hassam, Twachtman and seven other artists formed the group known as the “Ten American Painters”. The group sought an alternative to the established exhibition system and became associated with the development of American Impressionism.The artistic legacy continued after Weir's deathWeir died in 1919, but the artistic life of the property did not end with him.His daughter Dorothy Weir Young became an artist herself. She and her husband, sculptor Mahonri Young, later carried on the artistic tradition at the farm.New England painters Sperry and Doris Andrews followed them, extending the site's connection with working artists across generations.That continuity is one reason the property eventually became significant beyond Weir's own paintings.The National Park Service says the landscape was integral to Weir's artistic vision and to the development of a national style of painting. Today, the park's permanent collection contains more than 300 works, including paintings by Weir and Sperry Andrews and sculptures by Mahonri Young.From private farm to protected artistic landscapeThe transformation from a private Connecticut farm to a National Historical Park took place long after Weir's death.The site was established as a unit of the National Park System to preserve a significant place in the development of American Impressionism and maintain the landscape that inspired generations of artists.The present-day Weir Farm National Historical Park includes the historic home, studio and surrounding grounds. The National Park Service describes Weir House as containing original paintings, furnishings and decorative objects connected to the artists who lived there.The property's importance, then, goes beyond the unusual price paid for it in 1882.A painting and $10 secured Weir a piece of Connecticut countryside. He spent decades turning that countryside into a source of paintings, a home for his family and a meeting place for artists.More than 140 years later, the same landscape survives as a place where visitors can encounter the home, studios and surroundings that helped shape Weir's work and the wider story of American Impressionism.You use AI every day. DE NIRO SAYS HE CAN'T LOVE AMERICA, COMPARES COUNTRY TO ABUSIVE HUSBAND The FCC did not return Fox News Digital's request for comment. The liberal late-night host, upon returning to host his show after a summer break on Sept. 8, jabbed at Carr and said, "We're still here." articles.title: Carney pitches oil pipeline as a response to US-Canada trade war
articles.summary: A west coast pipeline project is the first to be fast-tracked and will be a major test of Carney's promise to global investors.
articles.body:
Mark Carney has announced that Canada will fast-track the approval process for a 1,250km (775 mile) oil pipeline project to the Pacific coast.

The Canadian prime minister argues the Pacific Link project is key to national interests, allowing Canada to diversify its oil markets away from the US.

"A pipeline to the west coast is part of our mission to transform our economy, to double our non-US exports over the next decade," he said on Thursday.

It will also be a test of his promise to global investors that Ottawa can move quickly to build major projects as he seeks to turn Canada into a global energy "superpower".

British Columbia v Alberta - how oil sparked a feud between neighbours

Carney said the project was expected to boost Canada's GDP by up to C$30bn ($21bn; £16bn) per year and create 140,000 jobs.

He argues that Canada's economic ties to the US have become a vulnerability in light of protectionist tariffs implemented by US President Donald Trump.

Last year, Canada sent 90% of its crude oil exports south of the border.

Pacific Link would be capable of carrying approximately one million barrels per day of crude oil from Bruderheim, Alberta, to a deep-water port near Delta, British Columbia.

The project includes the construction of marine berths able to accommodate vessels that can carry up to two million barrels-worth of oil.

From there, the oil would be shipped by boat to global markets.

Ottawa says the project will reduce Canada's overall dependency on the US to approximately 65-70% as it opens up the market to the Asia-Pacific region, including key markets such as South Korea, China, and Japan.

Pacific Link will be the first project to have its federal approvals and regulatory reviews fast-tracked under a new law put in place last year by the Liberal government.

The goal is to give investors a final yes or no on a proposed project within a year.

Fierce opposition and the country's lengthy and complex projects review process has contributed in the past some past pipelines projects being cancelled.

"People are watching very closely how Canada is handling this process," a government official said in a media briefing on Thursday.

They added that if it went as planned, they expected more private investment to express interest in the project, which is projected to cost between C$35.2bn and C$43.7bn.

The second hope is that the pipeline, which would run from Alberta's landlocked oil patch to the coast, will help appease the western province, which argues it has long been hampered from developing its resources.

Albertans will vote later this month in a referendum on independence.

Pacific Link was "a demonstration of the power of Canada", said Carney, speaking from Fort McMurray, Alberta, when asked whether he had a message for the province.

The pipeline project is likely to face pushback from environmental groups, especially over concerns about the impact on coastal marine health, as well as from some indigenous communities along the route.

Carney argues that discussions with many indigenous communities have already taken place, with "intensive" consultations to come.

The plan is for construction to begin by 2032 if it receives final approval.

Currently, the governments of Canada and Alberta are backing the project, along with one private investor, the Pembina Pipeline Corporation, which has a non-binding agreement for a 10% stake during construction and the option for another 10% once the pipeline is up and running.

A minimum of a 10% ownership stake will also be offered for purchase to indigenous groups.

As part of the agreement, Alberta has agreed to develop the world's largest carbon capture programme in a bid to reduce its overall emissions.

Ottawa has also worked to shore up ocean protection funding and rules to protect marine life that could be affected by increased coastal tanker traffic, including the endangered Southern Resident killer whales.

articles.title: Lawyer for Cornell accuser says university doctor was 'yet another failure'
articles.summary: Jane Doe told the school's doctor that she had contracted an infection "in a traumatic way", but they "didn't really follow up", according to the New York Times.
articles.body:
A woman who has accused several men of raping her at Cornell University in 2024 was failed by the school's health system, her lawyer has said.

Jane Doe, as she is known in court filings, said she told a university doctor two days after the alleged assault that she had contracted a urinary tract infection "in a traumatic way" but that they "didn't really follow up", according to the New York Times .

Her lawyer Thomas Giuffra said in a statement provided to the BBC that the doctor visit marked "yet another failure by Cornell".

Cornell said it did not have any additional information to share in response to an inquiry from the BBC about the health visit.

After Doe was seen by the university doctor, she said she was then told to go to therapy, documents from the institution's own investigation show.

"Ms Doe's disclosure warranted further inquiry, including a rape kit and consultation of medical professionals trained to deal with rape cases and a physical exam to document her injuries," Giuffra said in a statement to the BBC.

"Inexplicably, all the medical professional did was to advise Ms Doe to 'speak with somebody'."

The woman filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university in September, alleging she was drugged and raped by seven men at a fraternity house at the university in 2024.

She also alleged that Cornell failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved.

What we know about Cornell University frat house rape investigation

Cornell case highlights 'draining' maze for victims to report campus sex assaults

The case was referred to Tompkins County District Attorney's Office, the top prosecutor in the county, back in 2024.

District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said his office did not bring charges at the time because he had only seen a statement from Doe implying the incident was consensual and that she had not been drugged.

This week, Houten's office announced it would be re-opening the case - less than two weeks after Doe filed her civil lawsuit.

Cornell has said it provided evidence to the district attorney's office from its own investigation, including a Snapchat group chat in which fraternity members discussed a "free" sexual encounter with Doe on the night of the alleged assault.

Giuffra accused the district attorney of changing "his story so many times, I can't keep up with it" in his latest statement.

"The pattern I am seeing is that whenever evidence comes out supporting prosecution, he claims he never saw it," Giuffra said. "His defensiveness and attempt to save face has not been impressive."

Van Houten told the BBC that he had received a six-page statement from Jane Doe and the Snapchat messages from campus police.

But there was also a 120-page transcript from a recording of an interview by a Title IX investigator with Doe, with a victim's advocate, a counsellor and one of Doe's attorneys participating by phone, which Van Houten said he had not seen in full at the time.

"The full transcript – which I have now obtained – confirms the contents of Jane Doe's sworn statement," he said. "I have no intention of letting Mr Giuffra's unfair criticism distract my office from getting to the truth."

The documents from the university's Title IX review provide the most detailed account yet into the three weeks after Doe was allegedly assaulted and made the decision to report to the university. Title IX is a federal civil rights law mandating that universities follow certain rules when investigating sexual assaults.

The morning after the alleged assault, when Doe returned to her sorority house, she told her two roommates she had done drugs and had sex with multiple men, but did not yet use the word "rape" or "assault", according to the roommates.

She appeared to be "in shock" and "not really understanding the gravity of what she was saying", a roommate said, according to the documents the New York Times obtained.

The review also included Doe's text exchanges with one of the men accused of assault, who apologised to her after the alleged rape.

"I just wanted to apologize for how things went down the other night," he wrote. He said he and other men accused of assault felt awful for being too intoxicated to "shut it down and kick people out before it got way out of hand".

Her roommate told the university that as time went on, Doe "kind of came to realise that it was something bad. And that she didn't really enjoy her time there".

On 3 November, Doe texted one of the men accused of assault and told him: "let's be clear that 90% of what happened that night was not consensual. i was given more key than i can remember," she said, using a shorthand for ketamine.

"I know that i told u i felt uncomfortable and i didn't know anyone in the room," the text messages included in the document read.

Later, at the Title IX interview, she said she felt "100 percent" confident that she was raped, remarks her attorney confirmed to the BBC.

Doe went to get a rape kit on 7 November, three weeks after the alleged assault took place, but no DNA evidence was recovered, her lawyer said.

Giuffra said that if she had received a rape kit in October when she went to see the university doctor, it is likely there would have been DNA evidence.

The lawyer said the messages and other interviews from the investigation show that "Ms Doe's internal processing went from denial, to shame and ultimately acceptance that she had been raped by people that she thought were her friends".

"Her reactions were a textbook reaction to trauma," he added.

At the sprawling university tucked away in upstate New York, the tension on campus is palpable.

The BBC spoke to students and a faculty member at Cornell, all of whom asked to remain anonymous. Many others were reluctant and very uncomfortable to speak about the incident.

One female student, who is now a senior and was on campus in 2024, recalled how hard it was living there at the time, particularly as rumours began spreading about Doe.

Now, two years later, she told the BBC how she and her friends felt "overwhelmed" and "disappointed", comparing the atmosphere on campus to a "dark cloud". Cornell, she believes, greatly mishandled the situation.

A faculty member also called the mood "dismal". Staff were not trained therapists so it was hard to know how to navigate a moment like this, she said, and many of her colleagues felt at a loss for words.

articles.title: Putin warns West that Russia is ready to use every weapon to protect Kaliningrad
articles.summary: The Russian leader insists Moscow is "not threatening anyone" and is merely responding to statements by Western leaders.
articles.body:
Vladimir Putin has said Russia will use all weapons at his disposal if it considers its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad to have come under direct attack.

The Russian president insisted that Moscow was "not threatening anyone" and merely responding to statements by Western leaders that it was preparing for war in 2029 or 2030.

Throughout this week, Russia has accused Nato of preparing to blockade its territory, which borders Lithuania and Poland, warning that it would even be prepared to use nuclear weapons if the West tried to cut off Kaliningrad from the rest of Russia.

Nato has sought to calm the situation, stressing that it was a defensive alliance and urging Moscow to stop its "nuclear threats".

Western allies have faced a surge in so-called hybrid warfare incidents blamed on Russia, particularly in Poland and the Baltics in recent months.

Last week alone, Poland said a Russian helicopter had strayed into its territory adjacent to Kaliningrad and Lithuania said its population felt "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Thursday that his country was preparing for further hybrid attacks, "including serious ones", after a drone armed with explosives was found in August on the tarmac at Leipzig airport close to Ukrainian cargo planes.

Rosenberg: Putin shows no sign of stopping the war as Russia doubles down on Ukraine

In a wide-ranging speech at the Valdai foreign policy forum, Putin told his audience that he believed that international conflicts were highly likely to continue, but would get better as "Western hegemony" weakened.

Although the Russian leader himself began the full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022, he again blamed the West for provoking the invasion, arguing that Moscow had simply been forced to defend itself and take up arms.

He also insisted that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian economic targets were a direct response to Ukraine's strikes on Russia's oil refineries and its ships in the Black Sea.

"Now from every direction we're receiving calls 'let's stop'. But they started it," he said.

Putin admitted Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP. Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helped the Kremlin finance the war.

Russia has targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since the war in Ukraine started in 2022. Other civilian infrastructure is also regularly hit, with a key bridge in Kyiv attacked by drones on Thursday.

Putin also accused the West of instigating other conflicts.

"If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation, in this case we are talking about Kaliningrad but possibly some other territories, of course the issue of use by the Russian Federation of all arms at the disposal of our country will inevitably and immediately be on the agenda," he said.

He accused Nato of holding naval manoeuvres in the Baltic Sea that he argued represented serious threats to Kaliningrad. If the territory came under Western blockade, he said Russia would be prepared to use all means and forces, including nuclear.

"We are not threatening anyone. We do not intend to attack anyone in 2029, in 2030, in 2050. But if we come across an aggression we will have to respond. Citizens of European countries should be fully aware of that."

He added that while he was aware of the nuclear capabilities of countries such as the UK and France, the weapons at its disposal were unparalleled.

Western officials have long feared that, rather than invading Kaliningrad, Russia would use the relatively small distance between the exclave and ally Belarus - known as the Suwalki Gap - were it to attempt to seize Lithuanian territory by force.

Lithuania's prime minister told the BBC last week that his country had made evacuation plans in case Russia invaded and thousands of Nato troops are stationed there.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte made clear on Wednesday that none of the alliance's "exercises or activities" posed any threat to Moscow and that the Kremlin's messaging was "absolutely not called for and not helpful".

Putin spent some time talking about leading countries in the world having armaments at their disposal that could "swipe away all life or at least push the Earth to catastrophic consequences", and said that unfortunately no-one could be sure they would never be used.

He drew the analogy of a gun sitting on a theatre stage - if it was hanging there at the start of the show, it would certainly be fired at the end.

He appeared to call for the rules of warfare to be rewritten and warned of the increasing risk of artificial intelligence.

"The automation and digitalisation of warfare leads to its gamification. This leads to degradation and sliding back of humanity to barbarity," he said.

articles.title: Meet Nikhitha Swaminathan and Aanya Jindal, the Texas students who designed a new way to control heat in data centres and spacecraft
articles.summary: For two freshmen at Allen ISD’s Lowery Freshman Center in Texas, a science competition project has moved well beyond the school classroom.
articles.body: For two freshmen at Allen ISD’s Lowery Freshman Center in Texas, a science competition project has moved well beyond the school classroom. According to the Toshiba STEM Education Instagram post, Nikhitha Swaminathan and Aanya Jindal have been named national winners of the Toshiba/NSTA ExploraVision competition after developing an idea for controlling heat without relying on conventional active cooling systems. articles.title: Mum’s £217,000 dream home became a four-year ‘nightmare’ after neighbour demolished half of her Leeds semi-detached house, leaving her £80,000-renovated property exposed to rain, damp, mould and vermin
articles.summary: What was meant to be a family’s “forever home” has become a four-year ordeal for a mother in Leeds after her neighbour demolished his half of their
articles.body: What was meant to be a family’s “forever home” has become a four-year ordeal for a mother in Leeds after her neighbour demolished his half of their semi-detached house.Shivarna Mitra, 44, says the £217,000 three-bedroom property in Pudsey, West Yorkshire, has been left badly damaged and is now effectively unsellable. She had spent years saving for the deposit and then invested around £80,000 transforming the house after moving in in May 2021.But around 18 months later, her next-door neighbour Chris Rhodes began work on the adjoining property. Mitra claims the demolition eventually left sections of her home exposed, with holes in the walls and roof allowing water to enter.The resulting damage, she says, affected the home's electrics, carpets and wallpaper and contributed to damp and mould. She also claims rats, squirrels, wasps and other pests subsequently entered the property.She spent £80,000 creating her ‘forever home’According to SWNS, Mitra said she had spent more than a year looking for the right property before buying the three-bedroom house.“It was perfect for my family. It had a big garden for my son to play in and enough living space for him to grow up and for us to live comfortably,” she said.She invested about £35,000 in the garden alone, including Astroturf, decking and new fencing.Inside, she installed a new kitchen and carried out extensive decorating and renovation work, including new plaster, carpets and wallpaper. The loft was also fully boarded.At the time, the neighbouring property was occupied by an elderly woman. It was sold in July 2022 for £280,000 to Rhodes.Mitra said Rhodes initially appeared friendly and explained his plans for the property. But she claims their relationship deteriorated after she objected to his plans to remove the downstairs party wall.Neighbour says demolition was prompted by safety concernsRhodes submitted planning applications for two extensions in June and August 2022, both of which were approved by Leeds City Council.Mitra alleges the permissions were used as a pretext to demolish the adjoining property. Rhodes denies this.Construction began in October 2022, but Mitra said she initially had no reason to believe the work would cause such extensive problems.Her concerns increased in December when the roof of the neighbouring property was removed, leaving parts of her house exposed to the winter weather.In January 2023, she contacted Leeds City Council, claiming the work was not complying with the planning permissions.Rhodes has disputed that account. He said a storm had made the gable wall unsafe and that he removed it, along with another front wall, because he believed it posed a danger.He said he acted in accordance with Health and Safety Executive guidance and to protect people and neighbouring properties. According to Rhodes, the council only later told him that separate permission should have been obtained to demolish the structures.‘By then it was too little, too late’Rhodes continued work until May 2023, when Mitra says he was served with an official stop notice.By that stage, she claims, the demolition had already left much of the adjoining structure gone.“In the time he was asked to stop he had pulled down his side of the party wall and the breeze blocks, meaning I only had a layer of bricks protecting my house from the outside,” she said.“From the foundations, first floor, second floor, and up to the roof I am now exposed.”Mitra believes earlier council intervention could have limited the damage.“If the council put in the stop notice in January, there would still be the shell of a house attached, and I wouldn’t be as big of a mess,” she said.A new house was approved but never builtRhodes later sought permission to replace the demolished property. His first application, submitted in July 2023, proposed a five-bedroom house but was rejected.A second application for another five-bedroom design was approved in May 2024.However, the house was never completed. Rhodes subsequently sold the plot, together with the planning permission, for £115,000 to another couple in May this year.Mitra says she is not convinced the neighbouring house will ever be rebuilt and claims she has struggled to work with the new owners.Damp, mould and rats have added to the problemsWith the neighbouring property gone, Mitra says her own house has deteriorated.“Rats got in and chewed the wires, resulting in the house needing full rewiring,” she said.“Water has got in through the roof and holes in the wall and has caused mould and damp, affecting my son’s chest and my health but no one cares.”She says her heating bills have risen sharply because she has had to keep the heating on and use portable heaters during winter, with monthly costs reaching approximately £630.Mitra also claims walls have cracked and expensive wallpaper and carpets have been damaged. She says decking had to be removed after builders working on the neighbouring foundations damaged it, leaving rats underneath.Rhodes denies responsibility for the problems she has described.Council says property remains structurally stableLeeds City Council confirmed that the neighbouring property was demolished “without necessary permissions” after concerns about structural stability.However, the council said an inspection of Mitra’s property found that it “remained structurally stable”.“As these are privately owned properties, the council advised Ms Mitra to contact her house insurer and take legal advice,” a council spokesperson said.The council added that it would continue to monitor the site and take appropriate action if necessary.Mitra says she feels the council has not done enough and claims officials have not visited her property to assess its structural condition despite her requests.She says her insurer has pursued a legal claim, but she has been told the case may not reach court for another two years.‘I have nothing to show for it’The prolonged dispute has taken a toll on Mitra, who says she was also undergoing cancer treatment and recovering from major surgery during the ordeal.“I was really chuffed when I bought it – but the whole ordeal has been a nightmare, and it’s caused me to be very ill,” she said.“I have gone through cancer and had a major operation while all this was going on, so instead of recovering, I’m fighting battles from my hospital bed on emails.”She now wants to leave the area but says the condition of the property has left her unable to sell it.“I spent a lot of money to turn this into a house of my dreams, but now I have nothing to show for it,” she said.Rhodes said he and his wife had also suffered financially and emotionally as a result of what he described as “a series of unfortunate circumstances”.“There were very unfortunate circumstances that cost my wife and me a significant amount of money and stress,” he said.“This was a series of unfortunate circumstances that have created a bad situation, of which I tried to work with all parties concerned at every point to resolve.”You use AI every day. articles.title: SIT formed in Khargone to probe illegal cannabis cultivation on forest land; forest officials get notices
articles.summary: Khargone forms SIT after seizing 60 quintals of cannabis from forest land; Barwani and Khargone forest staff served notices, lease cancellations sought.
articles.body: Barwani/Khargone: A special investigation team was formed in Khargone district to probe large-scale illegal cannabis cultivation detected on forest land. Forest officials in Madhya Pradesh’s Barwani and Khargone districts have also issued notices to officers and beat guards, seeking written explanations over alleged negligence.Khargone superintendent of police Ravindra Verma told TOI that Khargone police have constituted a special investigation team after seizing 60 quintals of cannabis plants from two forest sites in Chainpur police station area. The SIT will arrest the accused, identify key players behind the operation and trace the supply chain, Verma said. Police are searching for four named accused.Khargone DFO Ramesh Rathod told TOI thathe had directed four range officers and 12 beat guards to patrol areas near the Maharashtra border, identify illegal cannabis cultivation and report it. Rathod said the forest department had not received any police letters seeking cancellation of forest leases or pattas. Once received, the department would prepare proposals and forward them to the collector.Sub-divisional forest officer Mukesh Merawi said divisional forest officer IS Gadria has issued notices to four deputy rangers and eight beat guards in Barwani district, seeking explanations for their failure to detect large-scale cannabis cultivation.Merawi, posted in Balwadi sub-division of Sendhwa forest division, said all forest staff had been directed to patrol forest areas regularly and immediately report any cannabis cultivation to the department.Following major seizures in the Warla police station area of Barwani, police identified farmers allegedly involved. Warla police station in-charge Narayan Rawal said they included Kalu Singh of Takia Pani, Micha and Kamal Singh of Dhokaliya Pani, Vachan of Adnadi and Khelajiya of Sonkhedi.Barwani superintendent of police Padma Vilochan Shukla said a letter has been sent seeking cancellation of forest land leases held by those involved. articles.title: Punjab informs Akal Takht of 7-member panel on anti-sacrilege law
articles.summary: Punjab govt informs Akal Takht of its 7-member panel on anti-sacrilege law amendments; next meeting Oct 6 to coordinate, seek feedback and build consensus.
articles.body: Chandigarh: The next meeting of the seven-member coordination committee set up by the Punjab govt to deliberate on matters related to the Jagat Jot Sri Guru Granth Sahib Satikar (Amendment) Act, 2026 will be held on Oct 6.The govt has also formally informed the jathedar of Akal Takht about the formation of the panel. The committee will discuss suggestions and feedback received from Akal Takht and work out a roadmap for coordination with its panel to build consensus on the proposed amendments.The govt appointed PCS officer Harjeet Singh Sandhu as nodal officer on Sept 23 to facilitate coordination between the two committees.The seven-member panel comprises former Jathedar of Sri Akal Takht Sahib Giani Raghbir Singh, Damdami Taksal chief Sant Giani Harnam Singh Khalsa, Sant Baba Sewa Singh Rampur Khera, retired Justice Jaspal Singh, retired Justice Gurbir Singh, retired IPS officer and former PPSC chairman Jatinder Singh Aulakh, and law officer Preet Inder Paul Singh.The Punjab govt constituted the panel on Sept 16 to coordinate with the Akal Takht-appointed committee and submit suggestions and reports on issues concerning the Act.On Thursday, Amritsar deputy commissioner Dalwinder Singh handed over the govt’s letter to the in-charge of the Akal Takht secretariat. The letter from the department of home affairs said the suggestions and guidance received from Akal Takht were being considered with “utmost respect” and that the panel would hold detailed deliberations and coordinate with the Akal Takht committee before giving the matter a “proper final shape”.The development follows a meeting between the panel and chief minister Bhagwant Mann on Sunday. articles.title: Peace marches & community events to mark Gandhi Jayanti in Pune
articles.summary: Peace marches, heritage walks, Gandhi Week events and community cleanliness drives planned across Pune to mark Gandhi Jayanti on Oct 1–7.
articles.body: Pune: A series of prayers, peace marches, dialogues and community programmes began on Thursday to mark Gandhi Jayanti in the city on Friday.At Maharashtra Gandhi Smarak Nidhi in Gandhi Bhavan, Kothrud, a week-long Gandhi Week has started from Oct 1 to 7. It will feature lectures, discussions, cultural programmes and films on Gandhi’s ideas, social movements, democracy and the environment.“The programmes would include prayers and bhajans followed by a peace march. We have been looking forward to participating in the various discussions taking place as well,” said Shraddha Jadhav, a Kothrud resident. Several other residents are also planning cleanliness drives. “We have planned to get children of the society together and conduct cleanliness drives in and around our locality to celebrate the occasion,” Vasudha Kulkarni, a resident of Wanowrie, told TOI.In another part of the city, at Aga Khan Palace, a heritage walk is scheduled in the morning, taking participants through the palace’s connection with Gandhi and the Quit India Movement.“We would explore the palace and brief participants about the Quit India Movement and Gandhi’s stay in Pune during this 1.5-hour walk. We usually have around 20 participants for the walk,” said Randhir Naidu, who runs Deccan Drifts.Pune Animal Liberation (PAL), an animal rights organisation, will hold a citywide Satyagraha march to liberate animals. The march will be held from Gandhi Bhavan to Aga Khan Palace. It will include public speeches, chalk art and street outreach conversations.Around 70–80 citizens are likely to participate, and PAL will also submit its memorandum of demands to the district collector Jitendra Dudi. Gajanan Thorase, a resident of Hadapsar, said, “I plan to participate in one of the Gandhian walks on Friday. I appreciate the Gandhian principles and philosophy and would love to know more about his life in Pune.”Safar Chhand plans another walk to explore iconic food outlets in the city on Friday. Some of these outlets date back to the pre-independence era. Parag Magar, the organiser, said, “Participants will discover food places and old eateries on foot. Celebrities and politicians have frequented many of these places over the years. articles.title: National team arrives in Kolkata for friendly with India
articles.summary: Endrick upon the Brazilian National Team’s arrival at the hotel in KolkataCredits: Rafael Ribeiro/CBFThe Brazilian National Team arrived this Thursday (1st)...
articles.body:
Endrick upon the Brazilian National Team 's arrival at the hotel in Kolkata Credits: Rafael Ribeiro/CBF

The Brazilian National Team arrived this Thursday (1st) in Kolkata, India, for this Saturday's (3rd) friendly against the home side. The players and coaching staff members reached the city after a flight departing from Brisbane, Australia.

The Seleção delegation received a warm welcome at the hotel where they will be staying ahead of the match. Hotel guests and team supporters formed a welcome line for the players.

The match will wrap up the FIFA international window for Brazil, who in this call-up drew 1-1 with Australia in Townsville and then beat the Socceroos 4-2. It also marks the first-ever meeting between the two national teams. Expectations are high among the local population, who are passionate about the Seleção.

Before taking the field on Saturday, the National Team will train this Friday (2nd) at the match venue, Vivekananda Yuba Bharati Krirangan Stadium, in a session scheduled for 4 p.m. local time.

Brazil and India face off at 11 a.m. Brasília time (7:30 p.m. local time) on Saturday (3rd), with live coverage on TV Globo, sportv, GE TV, and Globoplay.
